- What specific disclosures (e.g., premium yield trends, NIW market share, pricing commentary, reinsurance costs, loss ratio assumptions) should an analyst look at across the cohort to spot which issuer would be hit hardest by a new entrant disrupting pricing? (The question asks for a framework, not just the 2024 commentary.)
- (none — sufficient to answer the "what did the cohort actually say about pricing discipline in 2024?" part)## 1. Disclosures to probe pricing vulnerability

| Disclosure / metric | What it reveals about sensitivity to a price war |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Premium yield (net premium earned ÷ average risk-in-force, or per-unit premium rate)** | A company earning premiums well above the industry average has more room to cut before hitting marginal cost – but also more to lose from forced reductions. Track sequential yield trends. |
| **Persistency (12-month / rolling)** | High persistency (sticky book) shields current earnings from spot price declines on new business but means slower repricing. Low persistency forces faster commodity-like competition. |
| **NIW market share and concentration** | A player with dominant share in high-LTV or high-FICO niches may be defending a larger moat; a fringe player relies on winning on price and would be squeezed first. |
| **Expense ratio (underwriting expenses / NPE)** | High fixed costs amplify the pain of compressed margins. A low-expense operator can profit at lower rates. |
| **Reinsurance cost / structure (e.g., quota share, ILN)** | If front-end reinsurance costs rise (or reinsurers demand higher returns), the net margin on new business shrinks faster when gross premiums fall. |
| **Loss ratio ex-cat (or combined ratio trend)** | A loss ratio at the low end of the cycle leaves less cushion if rising volume pushes claims higher while rates decline. |
| **PMIERs sufficiency buffer (excess available assets over required)** | A thin buffer may force the issuer to raise premiums or pull back on new business during a downturn, but also makes them a less willing price fighter. A wide buffer is optionality. |
| **Single‑tier vs. multi‑tier pricing / pricing band granularity** | Finely segmented pricing (risk‑based) can be quickly adjusted; broad‑brush pricing may be slower to react but also slower to concede margin. |

When a new entrant disrupts pricing, the hardest‑hit issuers tend to be those with **high premium yields (most to give up), low expense efficiency, low persistency (volume‑chasing), and concentrated NIW in easily replicable segments** – especially if they also carry high reinsurance costs that cap net margins.

## 2. What the cohort said about pricing discipline in 2024

Across the six publicly traded MI companies, management uniformly described the market as disciplined, constructive, and balanced throughout the first two quarters of 2024. No issuer reported aggressive price‑cutting; many explicitly noted that competition remained rational.

| **Enact (ACT)** | “Pricing remained constructed through the quarter and underwriting standards were rigorous.” | “Pricing remained constructive in the quarter, and we maintained our commitment to prudent underwriting standards.” |
| **Essent (ESNT)** | “Competition within the MI industry remains disciplined” | “it's very balanced… a pretty prudent market, very constructive in terms of pricing” |
